newsitem.title: UK: West talks tough on Bosnia, many problems remain.
newsitem.headline: West talks tough on Bosnia, many problems remain.

text.p: As the large Bosnian delegation approached the table, Western officials held their breath -- would Moslems, Serbs and Croats all agree to sit together behind the Bosnian flag for the first time?
They did, but it was just a symbolic victory in the West's battle to persuade the various Bosnian communities to stick to the terms of the year-old Dayton peace process.

A two-day conference which ended in London on Thursday laid down the law to the Bosnians, telling them in no uncertain terms that they could forget about significant foreign aid to rebuild their country unless they fulfilled their Dayton obligations.
But the new tougher approach could backfire if the country's ethnic communities come to the conclusion that this new tactic -- known as "conditionality" -- is a bluff.

"I think quite frankly the trick will be establishing the measuring sticks and having the guts to do something adverse if the sides don't live up to their commitments," said one diplomat who took part in the talks.

The Bosnians promised once again to fulfil Dayton pledges such as establishing freedom of movement, handing over war criminals and forming common political institutions, aspects of the deal which have largely been ignored so far.
"All the communities are in favour of peace, but somewhat different versions of peace," international mediator Carl Bildt told reporters.
"They are trying to twist the implementation of the peace agreement to suit their own needs. That's why our presence is so important," he said
But the West has made clear it will withdraw its troops by mid-1998, leaving very little time for the peace process to take proper root and start healing the wounds of the 43-month war.
Hardliners in Bosnia will take heart from splits within the western camp on the best way forward and its failure to spell out exactly how conditionality would work.

The West's threat to withdraw aid if the Bosnians ignored the Dayton commitments raised the prospect of a country littered with abandoned construction sites, a vision which Bildt did little to dispell.
"I'm keen to avoid a stop-go process, too much micro-conditionality," he said.
"If we start a major project like building a power plant or a road, at what point would we stop or reverse what we'd done? We are still discussing this," he told reporters.
But diplomats said that even the threat of conditionality could persuade the Bosnians to toe the line.
"All these guys want money. That'll be the trade-off -- how far they will bend to get money," one diplomat said.

The main sticking point is the failure of the Bosnians to hand over indicted war criminals, but Bildt said decisions on what could be done would be left to the peace conference's permanent steering board.

Virtually none of the 75 people indicted by international war crimes tribunal in the Hague have been handed over and Bildt hinted at tougher action if the various Bosnian authorities did not hand over the alleged criminals.
"When they have had the time to consider this, the steering board will return to the issue. There is no doubt about that -- it's written in stone," said Bildt.
But Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic was unimpressed.
"Apart from the fact that all the speakers pointed out the need to arrest war criminals, nothing concretely has been agreed upon," he complained afterwards.

The conference agreed to give more money to the Hague tribunal to improve its intelligence work and track down the wanted men, a step which British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said he hoped would lead to more arrests.

But this could turn out to be in vain, given the reluctance of local authorities to detain the indicted men and the clear signal from major Western nations that they oppose the idea of forming snatch squads.
